## 7. Hidden signals

**The strategic statement was rewritten, and the new words are the tell.** In Q1 2026 the chief executive announced: "we have updated our strategic statement to better capture our focus, which is that Dave is a U.S. neobank pioneering innovative credit products for everyday Americans." Dave has stopped describing itself as a bank with a credit feature and started describing itself as a credit company. That is an accurate description of the economics — and it is the framing that makes the "this is a loan, not a fee" argument easier, not harder, for a plaintiff.

**"Fee" is doing heavy work.** Across six calls, management never describes the 5% charge as interest and never states an annualized rate. The words used are "monetization," "gross spreads," "net monetization rate per transaction," "portfolio spreads." Every one of those is lending vocabulary with the lending word removed.

**Coastal Community Bank is a regulatory structure as much as a funding one.** Management presents it purely as capital efficiency — lower cost of funds, freed liquidity. It is also a bank-partner arrangement, which is the standard architecture for asserting that state interest-rate ceilings do not apply. Neither call mentions that benefit. That omission is conspicuous given a Maryland municipality is simultaneously alleging unlicensed payday lending.

**A new voice, and what it signals.** Parker Barrile joined as Chief Product Officer in Q3 2025, tasked with "deepening member engagement through new product developments and strengthening our AI and credit capabilities." Within two quarters the debit card was de-prioritized and Dave Flex became the growth story. The product organization is being pointed at more credit, not at banking.

**The 2026 guidance embeds no further margin expansion.** Working from the raised guide: first-half revenue of $329M and adjusted operating profit of $145M imply second-half revenue of roughly $401M and profit of roughly $175M — a 43.7% margin against 44.0% in the first half. Management says as much obliquely: the investments "may temper fixed cost leverage over the next two quarters." The leverage story that drove 2025 is paused for the rest of 2026.

**A quiet pre-warning on revenue per user.** The chief financial officer explained that newly acquired members "begin lower and expand with tenure, more than doubling on average from the acquisition month to the fourth month on book." Because the company is deliberately accelerating acquisition, the mix will drag reported revenue-per-user growth down for at least two more quarters. It was stated plainly, and it is the most likely source of a disappointing headline on 2026-11-03.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** On operating evidence this is not a close call. Revenue per member, members, advance sizes, acquisition cost, payback period, credit losses, adjusted margins and cash generation are all moving the right way at once, and guidance has been beaten eight-plus quarters running. Capital allocation is disciplined and shareholder-friendly: roughly $207M of buyback in six months, funded partly by a convertible note issued when the stock was strong, with the balance sheet simultaneously being made capital-light through the Coastal Community Bank structure.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Not whether the business is good — it is. The question is whether the *price* of credit to this population is durable, because every point of growth above the underlying member count comes from raising it. The Federal Trade Commission sued Dave in November 2024 over how ExtraCash is marketed and charged; the Department of Justice filed an amended complaint on 2024-12-30 adding claims for consumer redress and civil money penalties; the case was still in discovery as of the 2026-03-03 call and management has said "no update" on three consecutive calls since. In late December 2025 the City of Baltimore filed a separate action alleging Dave operates as an unlicensed payday lender in Maryland, with effective annualized rates it puts above 2,500%, seeking to halt the product locally and refund fees. Management's answer to slowing revenue per user has been to raise the fee ceiling twice in 2026 and to push advance sizes above $500. That is the right commercial answer and the worst possible legal one. Size this position to survive an adverse ruling, not to a view that the ruling will not come.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and widening.** The moat is of two types and they are not equally durable. The first is an intangible-asset and scale-cost moat in underwriting: more than 136 million advance transactions since inception feeding a model that has gone from version 5.0 to 5.5 to 6.0 (now "more than 700 model features, nearly 400 of which are brand new"), with a short repayment cycle that produces an unusually fast learning loop. The evidence supports it — losses improved year over year while volume grew 27% and limits rose, and acquisition cost held at $19 while gross additions grew 32%. That is the signature of a widening advantage, not an eroding one. The second is a regulatory-licence moat: bank partnerships, payments plumbing, compliance infrastructure. It is real, and it is also the part under direct legal attack. Switching costs for the member are close to zero — management conceded more than half of its members use competing pay-later products. Hence narrow rather than wide.

**Secular threat: manageable.** None of the recognized structural decline forces bites here. Artificial intelligence is a tailwind to this business rather than a threat — the underwriting engine is the product, acquisition runs through brand and television rather than search, and management's argument that a weaker labour market *increases* demand for short-term liquidity is logical on its face. Payments disintermediation works in Dave's favour, since Dave is the disintermediator of bank overdraft fees. The terminal risk here is legal and regulatory, not secular: a court or a legislature deciding that a 5% flat fee on a fourteen-day advance is interest. That is a binary outcome on an undated docket, which is a different animal from a structurally shrinking base.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither — the honest answer is that **it is not cheap.** At $351.61 the shares trade at roughly 20 times the midpoint of management's own raised 2026 adjusted earnings guide of $17.00–17.50, about 18 times the 2027 consensus of $19.95, and roughly 15 times enterprise value to guided 2026 adjusted operating profit. Burden the earnings with the stock compensation that adjusted figures add back and the 2026 multiple is closer to 24 times. The screener's 17.5 times free cash flow — the single statistic that put this name in a value lane — is a one-time balance-sheet release wearing the costume of earnings power. This is a fairly priced high-quality compounder carrying an unresolved federal lawsuit, not a mispriced asset.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend widening · structural threat manageable.

Dave is a mobile banking app for Americans who live between paychecks, and on the operating evidence it is one of the best-executing consumer finance businesses in the public market right now. Its core product, ExtraCash, advances a member a few hundred dollars until payday for a flat fee; the underwriting is done by a proprietary cash-flow model the company calls CashAI, which reads a member's actual bank-account transactions rather than a credit score.

The bull case rests on five things that are all verifiable rather than promised.

Management has used the released cash to buy back roughly $207M of stock in six months, with $94M of authorization remaining.

Consensus for 2027 sits at $894M of revenue and $19.95 of earnings. On those numbers the shares at $351.61 trade at roughly 20 times this year's guided earnings and 18 times next year's consensus.

The optionality on top is Dave Flex, a pay-in-four card launched into member testing in 2026. Management says more than half of its members already use a competing pay-later product, that Flex targets roughly twice the credit limit of ExtraCash, and that it carries a similar margin profile. It contributes nothing to 2026 revenue and is deliberately excluded from guidance, so any contribution is upside to the published numbers.

Conditions that must hold for this case: the federal enforcement action must resolve without forcing a rollback of the fee structure; the removal of the fee ceiling in late August 2026 must translate into revenue-per-user reacceleration by the fourth quarter; loss rates must stay near 2.1% as advance sizes push above $500; and the heavier second-half marketing must convert into member growth rather than simply cost.

Pass for now, at a conviction of 2, and I want to be precise about why, because this is a good company and the verdict is not about quality.

Dave arrived in this lane labelled a deep-value candidate on the strength of one number: price to free cash flow of 17.5 times. That number does not survive scrutiny. Trailing free cash flow of $327M is inflated by roughly $80-100M of one-time working-capital release from moving advance receivables to Coastal Community Bank, which management quantified twice on the 2026-08-05 call. Normalized, the company generates about $205-215M, which is roughly 23 times the $4.8 billion market value. Four models pointing one way and one distorted statistic pointing the other is not a value signal; it is a data artifact.

Set the value label aside and judge the residual case on its own, which is what this lane asks. On quality the answer is genuinely strong. This is a business compounding revenue above 30% for nine straight quarters, adding 951,000 members in a quarter at a flat $19 acquisition cost with payback under four months, improving losses year over year while originations grew 27%, expanding adjusted margins to 44%, converting itself from a balance-sheet lender into a fee collector, and buying back $207M of stock in six months. I score the forensic file a 4 out of 5 and the trajectory as strengthening. There is nothing wrong with this company.

The problem is entirely price against risk. My reconciled fair value by the parts is $361 per share against $351.61 traded - call it fair. The favorable case reaches $490, a touch under the highest street target. The adverse case reaches $165, which is not an invented number: it sits just above the actual 52-week low of $152.21 and represents roughly 10 times adverse-case operating profit for a subprime lender operating under rate-cap challenge. So the shape is about $9 of upside to fair value against about $187 of downside, and there is no floor underneath - no deal terms, no tender, no net cash (the balance sheet carries about $16M of net debt), no dividend.

What makes the downside real rather than theoretical is the tension at the centre of this business. Every unit of growth above the raw member count since early 2025 has come from charging the same low-income customers more: the mandatory 5% fee in February 2025, the membership fee tripling in June 2025, the fee ceiling removed for new members in early 2026, removed for grandfathered members in the second quarter, and raised to $20 for the rest from late August. Five price increases in eighteen months, each buying less than the last - revenue per user decayed 42% to 40% to 36% to 24% to 11%. Meanwhile the Federal Trade Commission has been suing since November 2024 over how this product is charged and described, the Department of Justice added claims for consumer redress and civil penalties on 2024-12-30, and the City of Baltimore alleges unlicensed payday lending at effective rates above 2,500%. Management's commercial answer to decelerating monetization is the single worst answer available to it legally. Not one analyst across six calls asked about the case.

On the catalyst: I score it as a soft catalyst with no fixed date - the federal docket is undated, third-party and binary, and management has said 'no update' three calls running. Per this lane's neutrality rule that neither helps nor penalizes the score, and it has not. The verdict is driven purely by the residual value case: no discount, an unusually wide adverse case, and no structural floor.

On the moat: narrow but genuinely widening. The underwriting advantage is real - more than 136 million advance transactions feeding a model now carrying over 700 features, with a repayment cycle short enough to learn fast - and the evidence backs it, since losses fell year over year while limits rose and acquisition cost held flat at triple the scale. But member switching costs are near zero (management concedes more than half its members use competing pay-later products), and part of the moat is regulatory architecture that is itself under attack. On secular forces I see no terminal threat: artificial intelligence is a tailwind to a cash-flow underwriter rather than a threat, acquisition runs through brand and television rather than search, and Dave is the disintermediator of bank overdraft fees rather than its victim. The terminal risk here is legal, which is a different animal from a shrinking base - so I do not apply the melting-base cap, and I score the value case a 2 on price alone, not on durability.

Where this becomes interesting: $240 to $260 per share. That is roughly 13 to 14 times 2027 consensus earnings and about 12 times operating profit after charging stock compensation - a level at which you are paid for the legal binary rather than underwriting it for free, and which still sits well above the adverse case. The route there is plausible and the mechanism is already demonstrated: on 2026-08-06 this security fell 22% in nine sessions on a beat-and-raise quarter, because revenue came in a hair light. At a beta near 3.8 on 13.4 million shares with quantitative and index money that arrived only this year, one soft revenue-per-user print on 2026-11-03 gets you most of the way. Put it on the watch list with that number attached, and revisit after the third-quarter report.

interrogator_dossier:
# Dave Inc. (DAVE) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-09-22 · **Price used:** $351.61 (US dollars, Nasdaq listing, quote taken 2026-09-22; prior close $350.65)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-05-10), Q2 2025 (2025-08-06), Q3 2025 (2025-11-04), Q4/FY 2025 (2026-03-03), Q1 2026 (2026-05-06), plus the Q2 2026 call (2026-08-05) retrieved separately because the supplied transcript file stops at Q1 2026 and the most recent quarter is decisive to the story.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Dave is a mobile banking app for Americans who live between paychecks. Its core product, ExtraCash, advances a member a few hundred dollars until payday. The company charges a fee for it, and that fee — not deposits, not lending spread — is where nearly all the money comes from.

Across six calls the story has moved through three distinct chapters, and the shift matters more than any single quarter.

**Chapter one (Q1–Q3 2025): the re-pricing.** On 2025-02-19 Dave replaced an optional-tip-plus-express-fee model with a mandatory flat 5% fee, a $5 minimum and a $15 ceiling. Management described this as unlocking "enhanced member lifetime value through improvements in conversion, retention and monetization" (Q1 2025). The result was spectacular: revenue growth accelerated from the high-30s to 64% (Q2 2025), and average revenue per user rose 29%, then 42%, then nearly 40% across three consecutive quarters. Critically, the chief financial officer was explicit about the mechanism: "we're fully incentivized from a monetization standpoint to take incremental risk by moving people up the limit curve because we're getting paid for those incremental risk dollars" (Q2 2025).

**Chapter two (Q4 2025 – Q1 2026): the algorithm.** Once the one-time re-pricing had washed through, management introduced a new frame — a "growth algorithm" of "mid-teens member growth and low double-digit [average revenue per user] growth" (Q4 2025). Read plainly, that was a pre-announcement of deceleration: 36% revenue-per-user growth in 2025 was being guided down to roughly a third of that rate. The chief executive said so directly: "we expect growth to return more to normalcy this year" (Q4 2025). Two new pillars were added to fill the gap — a pay-in-four card called Dave Flex, and the migration of receivables to Coastal Community Bank.

**Chapter three (Q2 2026): the second re-pricing.** With the first fee change exhausted, management did it again. The $15 fee ceiling was removed for new members in Q1 2026, removed for "a large portion of grandfathered members" in Q2 2026, and raised to $20 for the remainder "effective late August" (Q2 2026). Maximum advance sizes are to be pushed "well above $500." The chief financial officer called this "a ton of room" and "stored energy within the business."

**What was quietly dropped.** Two things. First, direct deposit. In Q1 2025 management framed under-10% direct-deposit penetration as an opportunity; by Q2 2026 the chief executive had reframed it away entirely — "it's just not a strategic area of focus at this point." Second, the Dave Card. Card spend growth decayed from 24% (Q1 2025) to 27%, 25%, 17%, 9% and finally 7% year over year (Q2 2026), and management openly conceded they "deliberately shifted our focus from new debit focus initiatives." The "three pillars" framing has survived, but one pillar is now a stub.

**The through-line.** Every acceleration in this story since early 2025 traces back to charging the same members more for the same product. That is a legitimate and well-executed strategy. It is also, precisely, the conduct at issue in the federal enforcement action the company has been defending since November 2024.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Ninth consecutive quarter of 30%+ revenue growth" (Q2 2026) | Literally true. But the sequence is 64% → 63% → 60% (full year) → 47% → 30%. Thirty percent is the floor of that run, not its middle. | **True but framed to obscure a clean deceleration ladder** |
| "Durable growth algorithm… low double-digit [revenue per user] growth" | Revenue per user grew 42%, then ~40%, then 36% (full-year 2025), then 24% (Q1 2026), then **11%** (Q2 2026). The 2025 engine is spent; 11% sits at the bottom of "low double-digit." | **Delivered, but only just, and by re-pricing again** |
| "Adjusted [earnings] of $4.12, up 48%" (Q2 2026) | Correct as stated. But adjusted earnings add back $16.3M of stock compensation in the quarter — a real cost to shareholders of roughly $1.19 per share before tax. Burdened with that cost, the same quarter earns closer to $3.20. | **Real growth, overstated level** |
| Beat rate "6 of 7 quarters" (screener) | On earnings, yes. On **revenue**, Dave has now **missed** the Street twice running: Q1 2026 came in at $158.4M against $170.9M expected (−7.3%), Q2 2026 at $170.8M against $171.1M (−0.2%). | **The quality of the beat is deteriorating — bottom-line beats on top-line misses** |
| "Credit performance… further improving from an already favorable level" (Q2 2026) | The 28-day past-due rate ran 1.50% → ~2.21% (adjusted for a third-party settlement delay) → 1.89% → 1.69% → **2.12%**. Year over year Q2 2026 is genuinely 14 basis points better. Sequentially it is 43 basis points worse, which management attributes to tax-season seasonality — a consistent and plausible explanation given Q1 is always the trough. | **Honest on the year-over-year comparison; the level has drifted up ~60bp from the Q1 2025 trough** |
| "Raises 2026 revenue, adjusted [profit] and [earnings] guidance" | Verified: revenue $725–735M (from $710–720M), adjusted operating profit $315–325M (from $305–315M), adjusted earnings $17.00–17.50 (from $16.25–16.75). Eighth or ninth consecutive raise. | **Confirmed — this is the strongest fact in the file** |
| "Free[ing] up meaningful liquidity" from the Coastal Community Bank arrangement | Verified and material: cash and investments went from $121M (Dec 2025) to $176M (Mar 2026) to $253M (Jun 2026); receivables fell from $297M to $232M; the chief financial officer quantified "$93 million funded through the coastal arrangement" on a $225M facility. | **Confirmed — but see the free-cash-flow caveat below** |

### The free-cash-flow artifact — the single most important number in this file

The screener classifies Dave as a value candidate on one statistic: price to free cash flow of 17.5 times, on trailing free cash flow of $327M. That number is not a measure of earnings power. It is inflated by a one-time balance-sheet migration.

Because receivables moved to Coastal Community Bank, cash that used to be tied up funding advances was released. Management quantified it twice on the Q2 2026 call: cash from ExtraCash receivables "shifted from a $51.7 million **use** of cash in the second quarter of last year to a $30.5 million **source** of cash this quarter," and "we have already unlocked nearly $100 million of cash on the balance sheet." That is roughly $80M of swing in a single quarter, and it is not repeatable once the migration completes.

Strip it out and normalized cash generation is closer to guided adjusted operating profit of $320M, less about $45M of real stock compensation, less about $8M of depreciation, less roughly $60M of cash tax — call it $205–215M. Against a $4.8B market value that is roughly **23 times free cash flow, not 17.5 times**. The "deep value" label that brought this name into the room does not survive contact with the cash flow statement.

### Returns and leverage — the screener's fields are broken here

The screener reports return on equity of −28.2% and return on invested capital of −2.8%. Both are stale artifacts of the pre-2024 loss years and the special-purpose-acquisition accounting. On the actual June 2026 balance sheet, shareholders' equity is $208M against roughly $200M+ of annual adjusted profit — returns on equity near triple digits. Separately, the screener's "net debt −$46M" (implying net cash) is wrong: total debt is $268M (a $193M convertible note issued in Q1 2026 plus a $75M facility) against $253M of cash and short-term investments, so Dave carries roughly **$16M of net debt** on the cash-plus-investments definition, or $59M counting cash alone. Either figure is immaterial against a $4.8B market value, but it is a liability, not a cushion.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, and unbroken across all six calls.** This is not a management team losing its nerve.

- Q1 2025: "another record-setting first quarter, which outperformed expectations across key areas."
- Q2 2025: "our fastest growth rate in over 5 years."
- Q3 2025: "Q3 was another record quarter."
- Q4 2025: "2025 was the strongest year in Dave's history."
- Q1 2026: "2026 is off to a strong start."
- Q2 2026: "The business is performing exceptionally well."

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less: the 2026 outlook now carries three separately quantified metrics (revenue, adjusted operating profit, adjusted earnings per share) where 2025 carried two. Language has stayed firmly offensive — the Q2 2026 call is about leaning *into* marketing spend, raising credit limits, and going "well above $500" on advance sizes. There is no defensive vocabulary anywhere: no cost programs, no restructuring, no macro hedging.

The one place the tone hardens rather than softens is on competition and on artificial intelligence. Asked about rival earned-wage-access products, the chief executive was dismissive: "not worried about competition" (Q2 2026). On search and AI disruption: "We have no exposure to search or AI disruption whatsoever." Confidence at that level is worth noting, though on the evidence — record gross additions at a flat $19 acquisition cost — it is at least earned.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**High. This is the company's best attribute, and it is not close.**

The cleanest test available is the 2025 full year, which management themselves laid out on the Q4 2025 call: they entered 2025 guiding $415–435M of revenue and $110–120M of adjusted operating profit, and delivered $554M and $227M. That is 30% above the revenue guidance midpoint and nearly double the profit guidance. In dollars, $129M of revenue outperformance and $112M of profit outperformance — an 86% flow-through rate.

They have raised guidance every quarter for roughly three years. The chief financial officer was candid about why, in a way that is more credible than a denial would have been: "our goal is to put out numbers that we have very high confidence in delivering upon… want to give ourselves the ability to outperform" (Q4 2025). That is a plain admission of deliberate conservatism — sandbagging, stated openly. It is a feature for a shareholder, provided you do not mistake the beats for surprise.

**One deduction.** The pattern is now beating on the bottom line while missing on the top. Q1 2026 revenue came in 7.3% below consensus; Q2 2026 came in marginally below. Both quarters beat handily on adjusted earnings. Guidance credibility on the metric management controls (profit) remains excellent; credibility on the metric the market prices (revenue growth) has cracked twice in six months. The stock's reaction on 2026-08-06 — a roughly 22% drawdown over nine sessions from $430 to $335, on a beat-and-raise — is the market pricing exactly that distinction.

**Reliability score: High.**

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The question they will not answer: what happens to the legal case.** Four consecutive calls carry a near-identical non-answer. Q4 2025: "the case is currently in the discovery phase, and we have no material updates." Q1 2026: "we have no material update and continue to vigorously defend our position." Q2 2026: "we have no updates and continue to vigorously defend our position." No analyst on any of the six calls pressed further. That silence is itself the finding — coverage has decided the case is not worth modelling, which is precisely how a risk becomes mispriced in both directions.

**The metric that keeps moving.** When delinquency rose in mid-2025, management responded by changing which number matters. The chief executive opened the Q3 2025 call with: "Following last quarter's record results, we received a number of questions around delinquency metrics and loss provision trends. I want to clarify how we think about those dynamics… we are laser-focused on the net monetization rate per ExtraCash transaction." By Q1 2026 the preferred metric was back to "our 28 days past due metric, which we believe investors should use to assess true credit performance at Dave." By Q2 2026 a third measure — the 121-day loss rate — was introduced to rebut a question about the second. The underlying argument (maximize gross profit dollars, not minimize loss rates) is intellectually coherent and management has been consistent about it since Q2 2025. But the *headline* metric has been swapped three times, always in the direction that reads better.

**Pressed and later proved right.** Analysts asked repeatedly through 2025 about the JPMorgan/data-aggregator fee dispute — whether the cost of reading members' bank-transaction data would rise. Management deflected to policy hopes and claimed "significant pricing power" (Q2 2025). The topic then vanished from the calls entirely. It has not resurfaced as bad news, but it also has not been resolved on the record.

**What analysts are not asking.** Nobody has asked what happens to revenue per user after the fee ceiling is fully removed and advance limits pass $500 — that is, what the *next* lever is once this one is also exhausted. Management has now used two price increases in eighteen months to sustain the growth algorithm. There is no third one disclosed.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Insider selling is one-sided and heavy.** Zero open-market purchases against 78 sales totalling 450,859 shares. On a roughly 13.4 million share count, that is over 3% of the company sold by people who see the credit book daily, with not a single dollar of open-market buying alongside it.

🔴 **Every growth acceleration since early 2025 comes from raising the price of credit to a subprime population.** The February 2025 move to a mandatory 5% fee, the June 2025 subscription increase from $1 to $3 for new members, the Q1 2026 removal of the $15 fee ceiling for new members, the Q2 2026 removal for grandfathered members, and the $20 ceiling from late August 2026. Five price increases in eighteen months, into the teeth of an active federal lawsuit about how this product is priced and described.

🔴 **Revenue has missed consensus two quarters running** while adjusted earnings beat — the composition of the beat is degrading (Q1 2026: $158.4M actual against $170.9M expected; Q2 2026: $170.8M against $171.1M).

🔴 **The cheapness signal is an accounting artifact.** Trailing free cash flow is inflated by roughly $80–100M of one-time working-capital release from the Coastal Community Bank migration (quantified by management on the Q2 2026 call).

🔴 **The headline credit metric has been redefined three times** in five quarters, each time in the more flattering direction.

🔴 **Stock compensation is added back to the earnings figure the guidance is set on.** Q2 2026 carried $16.3M of it — about 29% of adjusted net income for the quarter.

🟢 **Guidance delivery is genuinely exceptional.** Eight-plus consecutive raises; 2025 finished 30% above the original revenue guide and nearly double the original profit guide.

🟢 **Customer acquisition economics are improving at scale, which is rare.** Q2 2026 added 951,000 members, up 32% year over year — the fastest in nearly four years — while acquisition cost held flat at $19 and payback fell below four months (from five months in mid-2024). The chief financial officer's framing is the right test and he passed it: "to see acquisition up almost at an exact same rate as our amount of spend… speaks to the… incrementality of that spend at nearly 100% at this level of scale."

🟢 **Credit improved year over year while volume grew 27%.** The 28-day past-due rate at 2.12% is 14 basis points better than a year earlier on a book that is a quarter larger — genuine evidence that the underwriting model is doing work.

🟢 **The balance sheet is being made capital-light.** Moving receivables to Coastal Community Bank converts a working-capital-hungry lender into a fee business. Cash and investments more than doubled from $121M to $253M in six months.

🟢 **Capital is being returned, aggressively and at scale.** Treasury stock rose from $43.7M (Dec 2025) to $251.2M (Jun 2026) — roughly $207M of buyback in six months against a $4.8B company, with $94M of authorization left.

🟢 **A structural overhang clears on a fixed date.** The chief financial officer confirmed on 2026-08-05 that "the warrant and earn-out securities expire in January of 2027, thereby eliminating the noncash gains and losses in our P&L." The $36.9M charge that made Q2 2026 reported profit look like a collapse is a countdown clock, not a permanent condition.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The strategic statement was rewritten, and the new words are the tell.** In Q1 2026 the chief executive announced: "we have updated our strategic statement to better capture our focus, which is that Dave is a U.S. neobank pioneering innovative credit products for everyday Americans." Dave has stopped describing itself as a bank with a credit feature and started describing itself as a credit company. That is an accurate description of the economics — and it is the framing that makes the "this is a loan, not a fee" argument easier, not harder, for a plaintiff.

**"Fee" is doing heavy work.** Across six calls, management never describes the 5% charge as interest and never states an annualized rate. The words used are "monetization," "gross spreads," "net monetization rate per transaction," "portfolio spreads." Every one of those is lending vocabulary with the lending word removed.

**Coastal Community Bank is a regulatory structure as much as a funding one.** Management presents it purely as capital efficiency — lower cost of funds, freed liquidity. It is also a bank-partner arrangement, which is the standard architecture for asserting that state interest-rate ceilings do not apply. Neither call mentions that benefit. That omission is conspicuous given a Maryland municipality is simultaneously alleging unlicensed payday lending.

**A new voice, and what it signals.** Parker Barrile joined as Chief Product Officer in Q3 2025, tasked with "deepening member engagement through new product developments and strengthening our AI and credit capabilities." Within two quarters the debit card was de-prioritized and Dave Flex became the growth story. The product organization is being pointed at more credit, not at banking.

**The 2026 guidance embeds no further margin expansion.** Working from the raised guide: first-half revenue of $329M and adjusted operating profit of $145M imply second-half revenue of roughly $401M and profit of roughly $175M — a 43.7% margin against 44.0% in the first half. Management says as much obliquely: the investments "may temper fixed cost leverage over the next two quarters." The leverage story that drove 2025 is paused for the rest of 2026.

**A quiet pre-warning on revenue per user.** The chief financial officer explained that newly acquired members "begin lower and expand with tenure, more than doubling on average from the acquisition month to the fourth month on book." Because the company is deliberately accelerating acquisition, the mix will drag reported revenue-per-user growth down for at least two more quarters. It was stated plainly, and it is the most likely source of a disappointing headline on 2026-11-03.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** On operating evidence this is not a close call. Revenue per member, members, advance sizes, acquisition cost, payback period, credit losses, adjusted margins and cash generation are all moving the right way at once, and guidance has been beaten eight-plus quarters running. Capital allocation is disciplined and shareholder-friendly: roughly $207M of buyback in six months, funded partly by a convertible note issued when the stock was strong, with the balance sheet simultaneously being made capital-light through the Coastal Community Bank structure.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Not whether the business is good — it is. The question is whether the *price* of credit to this population is durable, because every point of growth above the underlying member count comes from raising it. The Federal Trade Commission sued Dave in November 2024 over how ExtraCash is marketed and charged; the Department of Justice filed an amended complaint on 2024-12-30 adding claims for consumer redress and civil money penalties; the case was still in discovery as of the 2026-03-03 call and management has said "no update" on three consecutive calls since. In late December 2025 the City of Baltimore filed a separate action alleging Dave operates as an unlicensed payday lender in Maryland, with effective annualized rates it puts above 2,500%, seeking to halt the product locally and refund fees. Management's answer to slowing revenue per user has been to raise the fee ceiling twice in 2026 and to push advance sizes above $500. That is the right commercial answer and the worst possible legal one. Size this position to survive an adverse ruling, not to a view that the ruling will not come.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and widening.** The moat is of two types and they are not equally durable. The first is an intangible-asset and scale-cost moat in underwriting: more than 136 million advance transactions since inception feeding a model that has gone from version 5.0 to 5.5 to 6.0 (now "more than 700 model features, nearly 400 of which are brand new"), with a short repayment cycle that produces an unusually fast learning loop. The evidence supports it — losses improved year over year while volume grew 27% and limits rose, and acquisition cost held at $19 while gross additions grew 32%. That is the signature of a widening advantage, not an eroding one. The second is a regulatory-licence moat: bank partnerships, payments plumbing, compliance infrastructure. It is real, and it is also the part under direct legal attack. Switching costs for the member are close to zero — management conceded more than half of its members use competing pay-later products. Hence narrow rather than wide.

**Secular threat: manageable.** None of the recognized structural decline forces bites here. Artificial intelligence is a tailwind to this business rather than a threat — the underwriting engine is the product, acquisition runs through brand and television rather than search, and management's argument that a weaker labour market *increases* demand for short-term liquidity is logical on its face. Payments disintermediation works in Dave's favour, since Dave is the disintermediator of bank overdraft fees. The terminal risk here is legal and regulatory, not secular: a court or a legislature deciding that a 5% flat fee on a fourteen-day advance is interest. That is a binary outcome on an undated docket, which is a different animal from a structurally shrinking base.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither — the honest answer is that **it is not cheap.** At $351.61 the shares trade at roughly 20 times the midpoint of management's own raised 2026 adjusted earnings guide of $17.00–17.50, about 18 times the 2027 consensus of $19.95, and roughly 15 times enterprise value to guided 2026 adjusted operating profit. Burden the earnings with the stock compensation that adjusted figures add back and the 2026 multiple is closer to 24 times. The screener's 17.5 times free cash flow — the single statistic that put this name in a value lane — is a one-time balance-sheet release wearing the costume of earnings power. This is a fairly priced high-quality compounder carrying an unresolved federal lawsuit, not a mispriced asset.

**Rising, and increasingly offensive.** Q2 2025: "record performance... tracking ahead of plan." High. 2025 started with guidance of $415-435M revenue and $110-120M adjusted operating profit; the year delivered $554M and $227M. **Prepared:** 2026-10-12 - **Price used:** $368.42 (US dollars, Nasdaq listing, live quote 2026-10-12; previous close $353.40; 52-week range $152.21-$458.25)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q2 2025 (2025-08-06), Q3 2025 (2025-11-04), Q4 and full-year 2025 (2026-03-03), Q1 2026 (2026-05-06), Q2 2026 (2026-08-05).
**Continuity:** this committee last covered Dave on 2026-10-05 (price seen $346.57) and answered "pass for now" at a conviction of 2, with fair value near $361. Since then the only dated items are a Seaport price target of $422 (2026-10-08) and a 6% rise in the share price; no filing, results release or legal development has appeared. The next results date is 2026-11-04.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Dave is a mobile banking app for Americans who live between paychecks. Its core product, ExtraCash, advances a member a few hundred dollars until payday for a fee. That fee, not deposit spread, is where nearly all of the money comes from, and the story of the last five calls is the story of how that fee was re-priced.

**The re-pricing (2025).** A mandatory 5% fee with a $5 minimum and $15 ceiling replaced optional tips in early 2025. Revenue growth jumped to 64% (Q2 2025) and 63% (Q3 2025), with revenue per user up 42% and nearly 40%. Management was candid that this was a step change: the chief financial officer said the gross-revenue yield "has come from the pricing model change" and would "stabilize around the number that you're seeing today" (Q3 2025). The $3 monthly membership fee for new members, rolled out in June 2025, added a second layer.

**The algorithm (Q4 2025 - Q1 2026).** Once the fee change was lapped, management reframed the story as a "growth algorithm" of "mid-teens member growth and low double-digit [revenue per user] growth" (Q4 2025), and said plainly "we expect growth to return more to normalcy this year." Two new pillars were added: Dave Flex (a pay-in-four card) and moving advance receivables off the balance sheet to Coastal Community Bank.

**The second re-pricing (Q2 2026).** With the first fee change spent, the $15 ceiling was removed for new members (Q1 2026), removed for "a large portion of grandfathered members," and raised to $20 for the rest from late August (Q2 2026). Maximum advances are to go "well above $500." Revenue growth slowed to 47% (Q1 2026) and 30% (Q2 2026), still a ninth straight quarter above 30%.

**What was quietly dropped:** direct deposit as a strategic goal ("It's just not a strategic area of focus at this point," Q2 2026), and the debit card as a growth line (card spend +27% in Q2 2025, +7% in Q2 2026, with "no new initiatives aim[ed] at debit volume growth," Q1 2026).

## 2. Claims vs financials (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 revenue +60% to $554M, adjusted operating profit (EBITDA) $227M (Q4 2025) | Screener: 2025 revenue $554M, +59.7%; net income $196M | Matches |
| "Beat and raised every quarter for the last 3-plus years" (Q4 2025) | 6 of 7 recent quarters beat (86%); Q1 2026 revenue $158.4M vs ~$171M estimate was a miss on revenue but a beat on earnings | Mostly true; the revenue line has missed once |
| Credit improving while the book grows (28-day past-due 1.69% Q1 2026, 2.12% Q2 2026, -14bp year over year) | Gross margin 86.7% and expanding; net margin 35% | Consistent |
| "Unlocked nearly $100 million of cash" via Coastal (Q2 2026) | Trailing free cash flow $327M vs a normalized ~$205-215M | The trailing cash figure is flattered by a one-time working-capital release; the screener's 18.4x price-to-free-cash-flow is therefore too low by about a fifth |
| Balance sheet strength | 2026-06-30: borrowings $268M vs cash $253M = net debt of about $16M | Not net cash; earlier screener figures of "net cash" were wrong |
| Insider alignment | 0 open-market buys vs 78 sales (450,859 shares) | Insiders are uniformly sellers |
| Returns on capital | Screener ROE -28% and ROIC -3% | Distorted by the accumulated losses, convertible and warrant marks; operating returns are clearly high, but the reported ratios cannot be used as evidence of a moat |

Latest-quarter earnings per share fell 21% year over year on a GAAP basis because of a $36.9M non-cash mark on warrants and earn-out securities, which management said ends when they expire in January 2027.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, and increasingly offensive.** Q2 2025: "record performance... tracking ahead of plan." Q3 2025: a defensive detour - "we received a number of questions around delinquency metrics" - answered with a new metric, net monetization rate. Q4 2025: confident and defensive at once, with an unprompted passage on AI disruption. Q1 2026: "off to a tremendous start." Q2 2026: "performing exceptionally well," leaning harder into marketing and price. The language has shifted from "maximize gross profit" to monetizing "stored energy," which is confident but is also the vocabulary of a company finding more ways to charge the same customer.

## 4. Guidance credibility

High. 2025 started with guidance of $415-435M revenue and $110-120M adjusted operating profit; the year delivered $554M and $227M. The chief financial officer described the method openly: a "conservative approach to the guide, want to give ourselves the ability to outperform" (Q4 2025). Q2 2026 was the ninth consecutive raise. The caveat is that 2025's beat was powered by the fee change, which management itself said made that year unusually easy to beat. **Reliability: High.**

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- **Loss rates and larger advances:** analysts asked in Q2 2025, Q3 2025 and Q2 2026 whether losses were rising with advance size. Management's consistent answer is that losses are "an input, not an output." The 121-day loss rate "ticked up" in Q2 2026 per the analyst; management said estimates are better than a year earlier.
- **The Department of Justice case:** asked about in substance every quarter, answered the same way - "discovery phase, no material updates" (Q4 2025), "no material update" (Q1 2026), "no updates" (Q2 2026). The case targets exactly the fee mechanics that have since been raised further.
- **Data access costs:** the JPMorgan aggregator-fee dispute (Q2 2025) was answered with confidence in pricing power but no quantification.
- **Competition from larger neobanks' earned-wage products (Q2 2026):** dismissed on the grounds that Dave does not require direct deposit.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

- Red: five price increases in about eighteen months on a low-income customer base, each yielding less incremental growth (revenue per user +42% in Q2 2025, +24% in Q1 2026, +11% in Q2 2026).
- Red: the federal case and a City of Baltimore action alleging unlicensed payday lending remain unresolved while the fee ceiling is being removed.
- Red: insiders sold 450,859 shares on the open market with no purchases.
- Red: the subprime credit backdrop is deteriorating - the gap between the riskiest and safer high-yield bonds widened past 1,000 basis points on 2026-10-01 - and Dave's members are the most exposed consumers in the economy.
- Green: acquisition costs flat at $18-20 with payback under four months while new members grew 32% (Q2 2026).
- Green: 28-day past-due rate improved year over year through Q2 2026, with CashAI v6 rolled out to about a third of users.
- Green: $207M of buybacks in the first half of 2026 and a capital-light funding structure through Coastal.

## 7. Hidden signals

- The strategic statement changed in Q1 2026 to "a U.S. neobank pioneering innovative credit products" - the company is now describing itself as a credit business, which is precisely the framing the legal cases argue.
- New metrics appear when old ones look worse: net monetization rate was introduced in Q3 2025 just as delinquency questions mounted.
- A Chief Product Officer (Parker Barrile) arrived in Q3 2025 to lead credit products; Flex has been "test and learn" for three consecutive quarters with no unit economics disclosed.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: strengthening.** The operating record is excellent and corroborated. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is that the price already credits this: at $368.42 the shares trade at about 21 times the midpoint of guided 2026 adjusted earnings and about 23 times normalized free cash flow, with the federal fee case unresolved and subprime credit spreads widening.

**Moat:** a narrow but real moat built on proprietary cash-flow underwriting data and low-friction acquisition (no direct deposit required, a third of new members by word of mouth). It is widening on the evidence - lower acquisition costs and better losses at greater scale - but it is narrow because a regulator, not a competitor, can reset the economics. **Secular threat:** manageable; the AI-displacement argument management raised does not apply to a balance-sheet-light credit underwriter, and regulatory risk is a single-name legal matter rather than a structural decline. The cheapness case is neither a fear print nor a value trap; there simply is no cheapness at this price.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend widening · structural threat manageable.
thesis_evidence: The business claims are corroborated by the latest dated numbers: Q2 2026 (reported 2026-08-05) revenue $170.8M, +30%, a ninth straight quarter above 30%; members +17% to 3.08 million; 28-day past-due 2.12%, 14bp better year over year; guidance raised again. Nothing since (FMP news through 2026-10-12) disproves or impairs a load-bearing claim. The 6% rise since 2026-10-05 came from the general tape and a $422 Seaport target on 2026-10-08, not company news. The pass is about price against legal and credit risk, not about the business.
macro_fit_note: The macro read is reflation (growth up, CPI +3.35% year over year and accelerating) in a debt-cycle phase of discipline, where positive real rates reward cash flow now over long-dated stories with an expected horizon of about 18 months. Dave is a cash-now business (about 52% free cash flow margin) whose gross margin held up through 2021-22 inflation (80.0% to 84.4%), which helps; but its customers are the most exposed to sticky inflation and to the widening in the riskiest credit spreads, which hurts, so the net is neutral. Pass-through evidence: the fee ceiling was removed for most members and raised to $20 for the rest from late August 2026, and revenue per user still grew 11% in Q2 2026 (2026-08-05), so price increases are sticking so far.

grade_rederived.why: the expected return of 1.8% is below the 20% entry bar - wait for a better price, near 300.83

bull_thesis: Dave is a profitable, fast-growing consumer-credit platform priced like an ordinary lender. Revenue grew 30% to $170.8 million in the second quarter of 2026 (the ninth straight quarter of 30%-plus growth), adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding one-offs) rose 48% to $76 million at a 44% margin, and trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is about $327 million, roughly 52% of revenue. The growth engine has several independent levers: record member additions (951,000 in Q2-26, up 32%) at a flat $19 acquisition cost with payback under four months; removal of the $15 fee cap for most members and a plan to raise maximum advances well above $500; the new CashAI version 6 underwriting model, which management says delivers larger limits and lower loss rates in testing; a $3 subscription now paid by every new member (subscriptions 9% of revenue versus 6% a year ago); and the Dave Flex card, which is not in guidance at all. Funding is shifting off balance sheet to Coastal Community Bank, which already released nearly $100 million of cash, and management is using it to buy back stock - the basic share count fell about 5% in the second quarter alone. Management has raised guidance every quarter and beat the adjusted earnings estimate in each of the last three quarters. On consensus 2027 earnings of about $20 a share, 20-22 times earnings (a fair multiple for 25-30% growth with this cash conversion) gives $400-450. Conditions: loss rates stay in the current range as limits rise; the Department of Justice case settles without a business-model change; consumer credit does not crack.
bear_thesis: Dave lends to Americans who run short before payday, which makes it the most exposed name in the book to a consumer-credit downturn, and the regime read already shows credit markets fearful. Growth has halved from 64% to 30% as the one-time lift from the 2025 switch to mandatory fees laps, and the next leg deliberately takes on more risk: bigger advances, higher limits and a revolving credit card, with management saying the model is not built 'to drive the lowest possible loss rates'. The 121-day charge-off rate ticked up in Q2-26. GAAP earnings are noisy - second-quarter 2026 GAAP net income was only $6.7 million against adjusted earnings per share of $4.12, because of a $36.9 million non-operating charge our data does not itemize - and the loss provision appears to have moved into cost of revenue, which makes the gross margin harder to compare. The Department of Justice case has been in discovery with 'no updates' for over a year; a consent order capping fees or changing disclosure would hit the very pricing that drove the earnings jump. Insiders made 78 open-market sales (about 451,000 shares) and no open-market purchases. Short interest is about 20% of the float. At 12-13 times depressed 2026 earnings of about $13.50 after a credit or regulatory shock, the shares would be worth about $160-185.
consensus_delta: The market is not pricing terminal decline - it is pricing a consumer-credit and regulatory risk premium onto a business growing 30% with 44% adjusted margins. Street targets cluster at $422-500 (Seaport $422 on 2026-10-08, Loop $500 on 2026-09-08, consensus $435), which assume the earnings power is durable; the stock at about 16 times 2027 earnings assumes it is not. Where we disagree with the street: its targets imply 21-25 times 2027 earnings, which needs loss rates to stay flat while limits and products expand - we think 18 times is fair until the new underwriting model proves itself on larger advances. Where we disagree with the bears: the 2026-2027 earnings path is supported by pricing already in place (fee caps removed, $3 subscription) rather than by forecasts alone.
forcing_function: Results are the forcing function: third-quarter 2026 on 2026-11-04 and fourth-quarter/full-year 2027 guidance around early March 2027. A clean quarter with stable loss rates on larger advances and a 2027 outlook near the $900 million revenue consensus would defend the earnings base; continued buybacks funded by the Coastal funding release add a slower lever. A Department of Justice settlement without business-model changes would remove the largest overhang, but has no date.
valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three to nine months. First, third-quarter results on 2026-11-04: with growth slowing from 64% to 30% and a new-member mix that carries lower revenue and higher losses at first, a revenue miss like Q1-26's ($158.4 million versus $170.9 million expected) would hit a stock with about 20% short interest and a 3.9 beta hard. Second, consumer credit: delinquencies among paycheck-to-paycheck borrowers are the first to turn in a slowdown, and the larger-limit strategy magnifies the hit. Third, the Department of Justice case could produce a consent order at any time. There is no debt wall: net debt is only $16 million and funding is moving to Coastal's facility ($93 million drawn of $225 million at mid-2026).
positioning_washout: There is no mechanical seller base to liquidate - Dave pays no dividend and is not an index-deletion candidate. The selling pressure that exists is from insiders (78 open-market sales, about 451,000 shares, no open-market purchases) and from the roughly 20% of float sold short, which can swing either way around results. The 14% October decline came alongside weakness across consumer fintech and subprime lenders, a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off rather than forced selling, and a deeper leg of that same sector sell-off is what would deliver our $300 level.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near $300, which a sector-wide sell-off in consumer fintech as credit stress spreads could deliver. The shares have already fallen 14% since our last look, from $368 to about $322, but at our roughly $361 fair value that is only an 11% discount, short of the 20% this market backdrop requires. The thesis holds: the business keeps executing - 30% revenue growth, 44% adjusted margins, about $327 million of free cash flow over the last year, buybacks, and a guidance raise every quarter - and management's credibility is high (4 out of 5, steady trajectory, a narrow but real moat). What keeps conviction low is the risk profile: these are payday-adjacent loans to stretched consumers in a fearful credit market, growth is halving as the 2025 pricing change laps, GAAP earnings are noisy, the Department of Justice case is unresolved, and insiders only sell. Third-quarter results on 2026-11-04 are the next test; a clean print would not change the price we want to pay, and a weak one could bring the price to us.
sop_fair_value: About $361 per share (range $340-380), inherited from our 2026-10-12 review and still consistent with consensus: about 18 times 2027 EPS of $20.08, less net debt of about $1.25 a share. At $321.88 the shares trade about 11% below fair value.

No segment revenue block was provided, so no segment sum-of-the-parts.
risk_reward: From $321.88: about $147 of downside to the $175 adverse case versus about $39 of upside to the $361 fair value and $128 to the $450 favorable case. The pipeline computes the ratios from these levels.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note: Dave looks cheap against peers on earnings. The peer file (SoFi, Affirm, Upstart, LendingClub, Oportun, Block, MoneyLion, Chime) places it below SoFi, Affirm and Upstart and in line with consumer lenders at about 15.8 times free cash flow; at $321.88 it is about 16 times 2027 consensus earnings with 25-30% growth. Part of the gap is a fair risk premium for subprime credit and the open Department of Justice case, not purely mispricing. No peer override or anchor multiple is given, and the file flags no shared regulatory convergence, so the discount is treated as name-specific but partly earned.

# Dave Inc. (DAVE) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-11-02. Source material: five earnings calls (2025-08-06, 2025-11-04, 2026-03-03, 2026-05-06, 2026-08-05), the screener's financial trajectory, and FMP quarterly statements. Live price used: $321.88 (Nasdaq, USD, FMP quote 2026-11-02). Third-quarter 2026 results are due 2026-11-04 after the close.*

**Bottom line:** Dave is a small-dollar cash-advance app ("ExtraCash") with a debit card and subscription attached. Management has done what it said for two years running - nine straight quarters of 30%-plus revenue growth and a guidance raise every quarter - and the numbers corroborate the story. The two things a buyer must weigh are (1) growth is decelerating from the 60%-plus pace of 2025 to about 30%, as the one-time lift from the 2025 fee-model change laps, and (2) GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) earnings have become noisy, with a $36.9 million non-operating charge that cut second-quarter 2026 GAAP net income to $6.7 million even as adjusted earnings per share rose to $4.12.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
- **Mid-2025: the fee-model reset.** The 2025-08-06 call is about the switch from optional tips to a mandatory fee, which produced "our fastest growth rate in over 5 years" (revenue +64% to $131.7 million). The new $3 monthly subscription for new members was rolled out in June 2025.
- **Late 2025: defending credit.** By 2025-11-04 management was pre-empting questions about rising delinquencies, reframing the scorecard to "net monetization rate per ExtraCash transaction" - gross yield less losses. That is a legitimate lender metric, but it is also the moment the company stopped leading with loss rates.
- **2026: from repricing to scaling.** The 2026-08-05 call shifts the growth engine from price to volume and size: record new-member additions (951,000, up 32%), removal of the $15 fee cap for most members, a plan to raise maximum advances "well above $500", a new underwriting model (CashAI version 6, 700+ features), and a new credit card product (Dave Flex) that is explicitly excluded from guidance. Off-balance-sheet funding through Coastal Community Bank "unlocked nearly $100 million of cash."
- **Quietly de-emphasized:** direct deposit / primary-bank ambitions ("just not a strategic area of focus", 2026-08-05) and debit-card volume growth (card spend up only 7% in Q2 2026 versus 27% a year earlier).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Ninth consecutive quarter of 30% plus revenue growth" (2026-08-05) | Revenue $131.7M (Q2-25) -> $150.7M -> $163.7M -> $158.4M -> $170.8M (Q2-26), +30% y/y | Corroborated; but the rate has halved from 64% |
| Operating leverage, 44% adjusted EBITDA margin (Q2-26) | FMP EBITDA $91.2M on $170.8M revenue; FY2025 net margin 35% | Corroborated on an operating basis |
| Credit improving: 28-day past-due 2.12%, down 14bp y/y | Not independently checkable from FMP; cost of revenue jumped from $20.7M (Q1-26) to $47.1M (Q2-26) as the loss provision appears to have been reclassified into cost of revenue (other expenses fell from $36.3M to zero) | Plausible; presentation change muddies the gross-margin line |
| Earnings growth | FY2025 EPS $13.53 (+223%); TTM diluted EPS $15.42; but Q2-26 GAAP diluted EPS $0.49 versus adjusted $4.12 because of a $36.9M non-operating charge | Adjusted story intact; GAAP noisy - the charge is not itemized in the data we hold |
| Cash generation | TTM free cash flow $327M (about 52% of revenue), P/FCF about 15.8x | Corroborated |
| Capital return | Basic share count fell from 13.43M (Q1-26) to 12.72M (Q2-26), about 5% in a quarter | Corroborated - real buybacks |
| Balance sheet | Borrowings $268M vs cash $253M = net debt $16M (2026-06-30) | Modest leverage; funding moving to Coastal |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY - Stable, high
Tone has been uniformly confident: "record performance" (2025-08-06), "another record quarter" (2025-11-04), "performing exceptionally well" (2026-08-05). Specificity has stayed high on member and origination metrics. The one defensive turn was 2025-11-04, when management spent its opening on credit framing. Language remains offensive (leaning into marketing, raising limits, new products), not cost-cutting.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY - High
Management entered 2025 guiding $415-435 million of revenue and $110-120 million adjusted EBITDA, then "exceeded the midpoint of that original revenue guidance by 30% and nearly double the original EBITDA guidance." The 2026-08-05 raise was described as the latest in an unbroken run of increases on all metrics. FMP shows adjusted EPS beats in Q4-25 ($4.57 vs $3.31), Q1-26 ($3.64 vs $2.86) and Q2-26 ($4.12 vs $3.69); revenue was a miss in Q1-26 ($158.4M vs $170.9M estimate) and in line in Q2-26. The pattern is deliberate conservatism ("numbers that we have very high confidence in delivering upon"), i.e., mild sandbagging on earnings, less so on revenue.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- **Credit quality and loss rates** - asked every quarter; management answers with net-monetization metrics rather than loss targets. Q2-26: the 121-day charge-off rate "ticked up", which management attributed to new-member mix.
- **Competition from earned-wage-access products at larger neobanks** (Q2-26) - answered with acquisition data (flat $19 acquisition cost), not with pricing or share data.
- **Open-banking data costs** (JPMorgan aggregator fees, 2025-08-06) - "not a foregone conclusion that prices will increase"; unresolved.
- **The Department of Justice case** - "no updates ... vigorously defend our position" every quarter; in discovery as of earlier calls. Never quantified.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: Revenue growth halved (64% in Q2-25 to 30% in Q2-26) as the fee-model lift laps.
- Red: GAAP earnings volatility - Q2-26 GAAP net income $6.7M versus $57.9M in Q1-26, driven by a $36.9M non-operating charge.
- Red: Insiders sold 450,859 shares across 78 open-market sales with zero open-market buys.
- Red: Department of Justice litigation unresolved; regulatory exposure on small-dollar consumer credit.
- Red: Model-driven limit increases deliberately accept higher loss rates ("not necessarily to drive the lowest possible loss rates").
- Green: Customer acquisition cost flat at $19 with payback under four months.
- Green: Unbroken guidance raises; adjusted EPS beats in each of the last three quarters.
- Green: Off-balance-sheet funding with Coastal frees capital; meaningful buybacks (about 5% of shares in Q2-26).
- Green: Pricing power - $3 subscription and fee-cap removal stuck "with minimal impact on conversion or retention."

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
- The key performance indicator vocabulary shifted from delinquency rates to "net monetization" and "gross profit dollars" in late 2025 - a lender optimizing for spread rather than losses.
- Direct deposit was dropped as a goal in favor of being "top of wallet" through credit (2026-08-05): Dave is becoming a credit business, not a bank-account business.
- A new Chief Product Officer (Parker Barrile, 2025-11-04) coincides with the Flex credit card push, a product with longer duration and higher loss exposure than two-week advances.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
**Trajectory: STABLE.** Execution is excellent and corroborated, but the growth rate is normalizing and the next leg depends on larger advances and a new credit card - both of which add credit risk. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: whether third-quarter 2026 results (due 2026-11-04) confirm that larger limits under the new underwriting model raise revenue per member without lifting loss rates.

**Moat:** narrow - data and underwriting scale (CashAI trained on years of short-cycle repayment data), brand-driven low-cost acquisition (one-third word of mouth) and short payback. Returns on capital are positive on an operating basis (the negative ROE/ROIC in the scan is a capital-base distortion from accumulated deficits, not erosion), and margins are expanding, so the moat is stable rather than eroding. **Secular threat:** manageable - large neobanks bundling earned-wage access and regulation of small-dollar credit are real but not terminal; Dave is the disruptor in its niche rather than the disrupted. The current discount looks like a fear print on consumer-credit and regulatory risk, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
